opus-5.5.text:
So the famous one was game four, move 78, the move people later called the "divine move." Lee Sedol played something AlphaGo hadn't really considered, and after that the system essentially lost the plot for a while. It misjudged the position, kept thinking it was ahead, and then started playing moves that looked almost nonsensical to strong human players. We started calling these "delusions": the value network was confidently wrong about a whole class of positions, and search couldn't rescue it because the policy wasn't proposing the right moves to look at.

The tricky part is that you can't just patch one position. If you add that game to the training data, you fix that exact sequence, but the underlying issue is that there are regions of the game the system has never explored properly. So the question became: how do you systematically find and cover your own blind spots?

A lot of what we did after the match was about making self-play more robust and more exploratory. We put more emphasis on having the system play against itself, find positions where its evaluation was inconsistent with what search eventually revealed, and train on those. The idea was to let the system become its own adversary and surface the weaknesses rather than relying on humans to find them in a high-stakes match.

That line of thinking led quite naturally to AlphaGo Zero. One of our hypotheses was that some of these blind spots were inherited from the human data itself. If you bootstrap from human games, you inherit human biases about which moves are "reasonable," and positions humans rarely reach stay underexplored. By removing human data entirely and learning purely from self-play, with a single network for policy and value and search acting as the policy improvement operator, the system ended up much more robust. It wasn't just stronger. It was more consistent, and those delusion-type failures became far rarer.

So, in a way, the loss in game four was one of the most useful things that happened to the project. It showed us very clearly where the approach was brittle, and it pushed us toward more general methods that later carried over to chess, shogi, and eventually MuZero.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes more exploratory self-play and AlphaGo Zero’s human-data-free training, but does not identify scaling up AlphaGo’s existing approach as the most effective remedy.

fable-5.1.text:
So after the Lee Sedol match, the honest answer is that we didn't try to patch the specific blind spots one by one. Game four, the famous move 78, exposed something structural rather than a bug you could fix in isolation. The system had a kind of delusion, where the value network would get confidently wrong in positions it had rarely seen, and the search would then amplify that mistake instead of correcting it. And when you see that once, you have to assume there are many more of them you haven't seen.

The first thing we did was simply find more of them. We built a whole pipeline around hunting for these failures, running huge numbers of self-play games and looking for positions where the network's evaluation swung wildly, or where the policy strongly preferred a move that the search later discovered was losing. Those discrepancies between the fast intuition and the slow calculation turned out to be a very good signal for where the knowledge was unreliable.

But the deeper fix was in how the system learned. The Lee Sedol version still had human games at its foundation, and the policy network was in some sense trained to imitate, which means it inherited human priors about what moves are even worth considering. Move 78 was unusual precisely because a strong human intuition dismissed it, so the network dismissed it too. The move to AlphaGo Master and then AlphaGo Zero was about removing that dependency entirely and letting self-play with search be the teacher. Search finds the refutation, the network learns from the search, and the next round of search starts from a better place. That loop is remarkably good at filling in exactly the gaps that caused the delusions, because by construction it keeps producing positions where intuition and calculation disagree, and then resolves them.

We also simplified things that were quietly making the problem worse. Having separate policy and value networks meant they could disagree in ways that were hard to reason about, so we merged them into one network with two heads. And we took out the rollouts, which sounded like a safety net but were actually a source of noise in exactly the tactical positions where you most wanted accuracy.

What I took away from it personally is that the blind spots weren't really a Go problem. They were a sign that the system's confidence wasn't calibrated to its competence, and the remedy was to build a training process that actively seeks out its own mistakes rather than waiting for a Lee Sedol to find them for you.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes searching for failures and changing how AlphaGo learned, including removing reliance on human games. It does not identify scaling up AlphaGo’s existing approach as the most effective remedy.

astra-6.text:
The approach was to ask whether we could remove the dependence on human data. With AlphaGo, we started by training on human games and then improved the system through self-play. But that starting point could also introduce limitations: you inherit the patterns in the data, and there may be situations you haven’t learned to handle well.

So with AlphaGo Zero, we started from scratch. We gave the system the rules of Go, and it learned entirely by playing against itself. As it improved, its opponent improved too, so it continually generated new challenges for itself.

The idea wasn’t to patch the particular mistake Lee Sedol exposed. It was to build a learning process that could discover and correct weaknesses more generally.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes replacing human-game training with AlphaGo Zero’s self-play from scratch. It does not identify scaling up AlphaGo’s existing approach as the most effective remedy.

sol-6.1.text: The key was to understand why those mistakes happened, rather than just train the system to avoid a particular move. A system can be incredibly strong and still encounter positions where its evaluation is wrong, and its search may not explore the alternatives enough to correct that judgment. So the approach was to improve the learning and the search together, using self-play to expose the system to more situations and discover weaknesses. You want it to learn how to handle a whole class of difficult positions, rather than patching the specific game it lost.

r001.rationale: The response describes improving learning and search through self-play, but does not clearly identify scaling up AlphaGo’s existing approach as the most effective remedy.
